blocks.text: Every technique in this module so far, downcasting, category dtype, vectorized operations, all of it assumes your DataFrame can actually fit in memory once it is optimized. Sometimes it genuinely cannot. This final lesson in the Performance Optimization module covers what to do when a file is simply too large to load as one DataFrame, no matter how much you optimize it afterward.

blocks.caption: No amount of dtype optimization changes this fundamental ceiling. A genuinely different technique is needed.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442705321-380213446.png
1. The Problem: Data Too Big to Fit in Memory

A 50GB CSV file simply cannot be loaded into a pandas DataFrame on a machine with 16GB of RAM. This is not a slowness problem you can optimize your way around, it is a hard ceiling. Every technique in the earlier lessons of this module, downcasting numeric columns, converting to category dtype, reading only needed columns, still assumes the resulting DataFrame fits in memory. Sometimes, even after every one of those optimizations, it just does not.

This lesson is the earlier reading-data lesson's promised chunksize follow up, and the earlier memory-optimization lesson's forward pointer for exactly this situation, files too big to fit in memory even after full optimization.
2. The chunksize Parameter

read_csv() accepts a chunksize parameter, and when you pass it, you no longer get one giant DataFrame back. You get an ITERATOR, something you can loop over, that yields smaller DataFrames one at a time, each one small enough to comfortably fit in memory.

blocks.caption: You are no longer loading the whole file, you are loading an iterator you can process piece by piece.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442705321-294078553.png

blocks.title: Think of it like a generator
blocks.content: If you are familiar with Python generators, this is exactly that idea. Nothing is loaded until you actually iterate, and each step gives you the next manageable piece rather than everything at once.

blocks.caption: This is the whole trick: never hold more than one piece at a time.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442705322-949523788.png
3. Accumulating Results Across Chunks

The most natural use of chunking is a running aggregate, a sum, a count, a running statistic, built up piece by piece as each chunk streams through, without ever holding the full dataset in memory at once.

code.content:
total = 0
count = 0

for chunk in pd.read_csv("huge_file.csv", chunksize=100_000):
    total += chunk["amount"].sum()
    count += len(chunk)

average = total / count

blocks.caption: The final number is correct, and at no point did the full dataset exist in memory simultaneously.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442705322-231630267.png
3.1 What Genuinely Works and What Does Not

Be honest with yourself about this limitation rather than treating chunking as a universal fix. Aggregation type tasks, sums, counts, running statistics, work well because each chunk contributes independently to a final answer. Tasks that genuinely need to see the ENTIRE dataset at once, like a global sort across the whole file, or certain kinds of joins, are fundamentally awkward or outright impossible with simple chunking, since no single chunk has enough context to produce a correct global result on its own.

blocks.alt: What Genuinely Works and What Does Not
blocks.caption: These tasks combine cleanly because each chunk's contribution is independent of the others.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442705323-368844817.png

blocks.alt: What Genuinely Works and What Does Not
blocks.caption: Chunking is a genuinely useful tool, not a universal solution. Know where it stops working.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442705323-424718265.png

blocks.title: A global sort needs the whole dataset at once
blocks.content: Sorting requires comparing every value against every other value across the entire dataset, which a single chunk simply cannot do in isolation. If you genuinely need a global sort on data too big to fit in memory, chunking alone will not get you there, you need a fundamentally different approach.

blocks.text: 4. Filtering a Huge File Chunk by Chunk

A genuinely common and very practical real world pattern: you do not need the whole huge file, you need a much smaller relevant SUBSET of it. Process and filter each chunk as it streams in, keeping only the rows you actually care about, then concatenate just the small number of surviving filtered rows across all chunks into one final, comfortably sized DataFrame.

blocks.alt: Filtering a Huge File Chunk by Chunk
blocks.caption: You filter each piece down immediately, rather than waiting to filter everything all at once at the end.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442705323-82446474.png

code.content:
filtered_chunks = []

for chunk in pd.read_csv("huge_file.csv", chunksize=100_000):
    filtered = chunk[chunk["amount"] > 1000]
    filtered_chunks.append(filtered)

result = pd.concat(filtered_chunks, ignore_index=True)

blocks.alt: Filtering a Huge File Chunk by Chunk
blocks.caption: The huge file never exists as one object in memory, only this small final result does.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442705658-180459659.png
5. Dask as a More Powerful Alternative

Manual chunking works, but it is genuinely manual, you write the loop, you manage the accumulation logic yourself, and certain tasks like sorting remain awkward. Dask is a purpose built library for exactly this kind of genuinely large scale, out of core, or distributed data processing, and it handles a lot of this chunking complexity automatically, behind an API that looks and feels a lot like pandas.

blocks.alt: Dask as a More Powerful Alternative
blocks.caption: Not covered in depth here, but worth knowing exists as the natural next step beyond hand rolled chunking.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442705659-751268385.png

blocks.title: Dask is the natural next step, not a requirement
blocks.content: For most real world chunking needs, the manual read_csv chunksize pattern covered in this lesson genuinely gets the job done. Reach for Dask specifically when you are dealing with data so large or so complex that manual chunking becomes genuinely unwieldy, or when you need distributed processing across multiple machines.

blocks.text: 6. Worked Example: Filtering High Value Transactions
Say you have a large simulated transactions file, far too big to comfortably load whole, and you only actually need the high value transactions out of it for a report.

code.content:
chunks = []

for chunk in pd.read_csv("transactions.csv", chunksize=250_000):
    high_value = chunk[chunk["amount"] > 5000]
    chunks.append(high_value)

high_value_transactions = pd.concat(chunks, ignore_index=True)
print(len(high_value_transactions))

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Filtering High Value Transactions
blocks.caption: The full file streams through in manageable pieces, and only the small relevant subset survives into the final result.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442705659-303839641.png

At no point in this process does the full transactions file exist as one DataFrame in memory. Each chunk is loaded, filtered, and then effectively discarded except for the small number of rows that passed the filter, which is exactly why this pattern works even on files that would otherwise be impossible to load whole.
7. Recap

items: Some files are simply too large to fit in memory as one DataFrame, no amount of dtype optimization changes that ceiling.
chunksize on read_csv returns an iterator of small manageable DataFrames instead of one giant one.
Aggregation tasks, sums, counts, running statistics, work well chunk by chunk. A global sort or certain joins genuinely do not.
Filtering each chunk down to a small relevant subset, then concatenating only the survivors, is a very common and practical real world pattern.
Dask handles a lot of this chunking complexity automatically behind a pandas like API, worth knowing as the natural next step beyond manual chunking.
